flashcards.q: Why does a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine freeze the ENTIRE event loop, not just that coroutine?
flashcards.a: The event loop is single-threaded and only switches between coroutines at await points. A blocking call with no await never yields control, so nothing else registered with the loop can make progress until it finishes, regardless of how many tasks were defined as 'concurrent'.

flashcards.q: What does task.cancel() actually do, mechanically?
flashcards.a: It schedules a CancelledError to be raised at the task's NEXT suspension point (next await) -- not immediately. A task with no await inside it cannot be cancelled at all until it reaches one.

flashcards.q: Why is swallowing CancelledError without re-raising dangerous?
flashcards.a: If caught without re-raising, the enclosing Task reports as completed normally (or with a different exception), not as cancelled -- any caller checking task.cancelled() or relying on cancellation propagating (e.g. a TaskGroup) gets silently wrong behavior.

flashcards.q: What guarantee does TaskGroup provide that gather() does not?
flashcards.a: Every task either completes or is cancelled before the async with block exits; one task's exception auto-cancels all siblings and ALL exceptions are collected into one ExceptionGroup. gather() (without return_exceptions=True) re-raises only the first exception and doesn't guarantee siblings are cleanly cancelled/awaited.

No. return_exceptions=True collects every result/exception into the returned list, but does NOT auto-cancel siblings on failure -- every task still runs to completion regardless. TaskGroup auto-cancels siblings the moment any task fails. Different tradeoffs.

flashcards.q: Why is a semaphore insufficient to respect a downstream API's requests-per-second rate limit?
flashcards.a: A semaphore caps CONCURRENCY (in-flight count), not RATE (throughput over time). Fast-completing requests under a low concurrency cap can still exceed a per-second rate limit. Token-bucket rate limiting caps the actual start rate directly.

flashcards.q: Why is backpressure not automatic in asyncio, and what's the standard fix?
flashcards.a: An unbounded asyncio.Queue or unthrottled create_task() loop accepts work indefinitely, growing memory unboundedly if the consumer falls behind. Fix: a bounded queue (maxsize=N), where put() itself suspends the producer once full, directly coupling producer speed to consumer speed.

It lets structured-concurrency constructs (TaskGroup, asyncio.timeout()) scope a cancellation to just their own block, distinguishing 'this timeout deadline fired' from 'someone cancelled the whole outer task' -- a distinction pre-3.11 cancellation handling couldn't cleanly make.

flashcards.q: Why does asyncio give zero speedup for CPU-bound work?
flashcards.a: Asyncio's concurrency comes entirely from suspending at await points while waiting on I/O -- it runs on one thread. CPU-bound code never awaits, so it just runs to completion on that one thread with zero parallelism regardless of how many coroutines exist. Use ProcessPoolExecutor or free-threaded Python instead.
